vignette:
She is twenty-one, North American, and works as an electrician apprentice, the kind of person who is used to climbing ladders before most people have had coffee. She likes the feeling of doing something physical and exact, of knowing where each wire goes, of making a system work. Before the accident, she describes herself as independent and hard to rattle. She drives herself from site to site in an old pickup with tools sliding in the back, eats gas-station breakfasts, and jokes easily with the older men on the crew. She is single and lives alone in a small apartment she keeps mostly neat, work boots by the door.

The collision happens at the end of a long day. It is raining, the kind that makes the road shine black under oncoming headlights. She is driving home from a job outside the city, tired but thinking about ordinary things-whether she remembered to text her foreman back, whether she has enough groceries for the week. At an intersection, another vehicle runs the light. She does not have time to fully understand what she is seeing before there is a violent impact on the driver's side. Metal folds inward. Glass bursts across her lap and into her hair. For a few seconds, maybe longer, everything is noise-horn, crunching steel, a scream she later realizes is her own.

She remembers the smell most clearly: gasoline, hot rubber, the burnt-air smell of deployed airbags. Her chest is pinned by the seat belt. She tries to move her left leg and cannot. She thinks, with sudden plain certainty, I'm going to die here. She hears voices outside the truck but cannot make out words. Rain is coming through the broken window, cold on her face. She is afraid the vehicle will catch fire before anyone gets her out. By the time paramedics reach her, she is shaking so hard her teeth knock together. In the emergency department, she is told she is lucky-no spinal injury, no major internal damage, only fractures and bruising and a concussion. The word lucky lands strangely. For weeks afterward, she thinks about how close metal came to her body.

Her physical recovery is straightforward compared with what follows. At first everyone around her is focused on whether she can walk comfortably again, when she can return to work, whether the insurance claim will go through. She tells people she is fine because she believes she should be. But sleep becomes unfamiliar. She wakes with her heart racing, hearing the impact again before she is fully awake. Sometimes she dreams the truck is filling with water instead of rain, and she claws at the sheets before she knows where she is. During the day, flashes of the accident intrude without warning: a car entering an intersection too fast, the hiss of air brakes, the smell of wet pavement. Her body reacts before her mind catches up. Her hands sweat, shoulders lock, stomach drops.

When she is finally cleared to return to work, she thinks getting back to routine will fix it. Instead, the drive to job sites becomes its own ordeal. She leaves absurdly early so she can avoid traffic. She grips the steering wheel until her wrists ache. At yellow lights she feels a jolt of panic and brakes hard, earning angry honks from drivers behind her. If a vehicle edges into an intersection, she stops breathing. More than once she has to pull onto the shoulder because she is suddenly dizzy and sure another crash is about to happen. She starts making excuses to trade jobs with coworkers so she can stay on one site longer and avoid driving across town.

At work she is still competent, but she is no longer easygoing. Loud bangs-dropped conduit, a slammed panel door-make her flinch so visibly that others notice. She scans parking lots before getting into her truck. She chooses spots where she can pull straight out, never reverse. If rain starts while she is on a site, her concentration frays. She tells herself to focus on the circuit, on the meter reading, on the sequence she knows by heart, but part of her is back in that intersection, waiting for impact.

Outside work, her life narrows. She turns down invitations because going anywhere means being on the road, especially at night. Friends tease her for "ghosting," and she does not know how to explain that even being a passenger feels unbearable; she watches every cross street and silently braces her feet against the floorboard. She is more irritable with her mother on the phone, more distant with everyone. She used to stop for coffee after shifts or wander hardware stores on weekends. Now she goes straight home and locks the door.

What troubles her almost as much as the fear is the change in how she sees herself. She feels ashamed of being jumpy, ashamed that a simple commute can undo her. She tells herself other people survive worse. And yet her body does not believe she is safe. She keeps replaying tiny details from the collision, as if finding the exact moment when everything went wrong could somehow make the world predictable again. Months later, she is still exhausted from sleeping lightly, still on guard at intersections, still organizing her days around what roads she can avoid. She speaks about the accident matter-of-factly at first, but underneath is the ongoing sense that life divided sharply that evening: the person who drove without thinking, and the person who now measures every trip against the possibility of not making it home.
